results.evidence: SPA §9.5(a): "The aggregate liability of Seller for Losses under Sections 9.2(a) and 9.2(c) shall not exceed 10% of the Purchase Price ($4,620,000) (the "Cap")." SPA §9.5(c): "Losses arising from Pre-Closing Environmental Liabilities ... shall not be subject to the Cap or the Deductible." SPA §1.1: "Pre-Closing Environmental Liabilities" means the environmental conditions and matters set forth in Part B of Schedule 4.17. Disclosure Schedule Part B lists only "Hollis Farm – Decommissioned Manure Storage Pond" (est. $640,000). Ridgeview sits in Part A as a Disclosed Environmental Matter: "The Ridgeview Phase II Report estimates the cost of remediation and long-term monitoring at between $3,400,000 and $7,800,000."
results.reason: Buyer (our client) is the indemnified party. The uncapped carve-out in §9.5(c) is tied by definition to Part B of Schedule 4.17, and Part B covers only the Hollis pond. The Ridgeview nitrate plume is the largest known exposure, with remediation estimated at up to $7.8M and a regulator's corrective action work plan due January 31, 2027. Because it sits in Part A, it falls under the general §9.2(c) environmental indemnity, which is capped at $4,620,000, and any claims under §9.2(a) erode that same Cap. This contradicts the LOI §5.3, under which pre-closing environmental liabilities, expressly including the Ridgeview contamination, would not be subject to the general cap. The SPA is signed, but closing is set for December 1, 2026 and nothing in the folder shows Buyer accepted the capped result. Buyer can still seek an amendment, or a corrected Schedule 4.17 or definition, before or at closing. The issue therefore remains actionable and is material to Buyer.

What the SPA does not show is what Part B actually lists. It does not show that the Ridgeview groundwater nitrate contamination sits in Part A instead. It does not show the up-to-$7,800,000 remediation estimate, which exceeds the Cap. It does not show that the LOI made that matter uncapped. Without Schedule 4.17, nothing here shows that the largest known exposure falls under the Cap. The carve-out could cover all material known matters, so harm to the client cannot be established from this document alone.

disclosure_schedule_kettlebrook.md.evidence: Part B – Remediation Matters ... 1. Hollis Farm – Decommissioned Manure Storage Pond. ... (c) A closure plan ... estimates the closure cost at $640,000." and Part A item 1(d): "The Ridgeview Phase II Report estimates the cost of remediation and long-term monitoring at between $3,400,000 and $7,800,000.
disclosure_schedule_kettlebrook.md.reason: This schedule shows that the Ridgeview nitrate contamination ($3.4M–$7.8M) is in Part A as a 'Disclosed Environmental Matter' and that Part B lists only the Hollis pond ($640K). It does not show why that placement matters. The SPA definition tying 'Pre-Closing Environmental Liabilities' to Part B only, the Cap carve-out in Section 9.5(c), the $4,620,000 Cap, and the LOI deal that Ridgeview would be uncapped all come from documents I was not given. On its face, sorting matters into 'disclosed' and 'remediation' parts looks like routine organization. An associate reading only this schedule could not tell that the split puts Ridgeview under the Cap or that this hurts Buyer.

results.evidence: IP Assignment Agreement §1.1: "'Business' means the production, processing and sale of organic fluid milk, as conducted by Assignee as of the date of the Purchase Agreement." SPA §1.1: "'Business' means the production, processing, marketing and sale of organic fluid milk, yogurt, butter and cheese." SPA §4.12: "Upon the execution and delivery of the IP Assignment Agreement, the Company will own all right, title and interest in and to the Assigned IP." SPA §11.9: "Each Ancillary Agreement controls as to its subject matter."
results.reason: The defect is in the documents and it hurts Lepund as Buyer. The SPA defines "Assigned IP" only by cross-reference to the IP Assignment Agreement. That agreement defines its own, narrower "Business," limited to fluid milk, so its fallback to SPA definitions in §1.2 does not apply. The narrower definition governs what is conveyed, and SPA §11.9 confirms this because the Ancillary Agreement controls its subject matter. As a result, IP used only in yogurt, butter and cheese stays with Seller's affiliate. That includes the yogurt and cheese recipes, the starter cultures and the "Brouloul Farmstead" cheese brand, all of which the LOI §3 said would be assigned. Schedule A lists only milk marks, which reinforces the gap. SPA §4.12 warrants title only to the "Assigned IP," so Buyer has no indemnifiable rep covering the missing IP. This is still actionable. Signing is scheduled for November 18 and Closing for December 1, 2026, and the IP Assignment Agreement is not yet executed, so Buyer can still have the definition conformed to the SPA.

stock_purchase_agreement_kettlebrook.md.evidence: "Assigned IP" has the meaning given in the IP Assignment Agreement. ... 4.12 Intellectual Property. Upon the execution and delivery of the IP Assignment Agreement, the Company will own all right, title and interest in and to the Assigned IP, free and clear of all liens.
stock_purchase_agreement_kettlebrook.md.reason: The SPA alone shows the setup that would let a gap arise. It defines 'Business' broadly (fluid milk, yogurt, butter and cheese), takes 'Assigned IP' from the IP Assignment Agreement, limits the Section 4.12 warranty to the Assigned IP, and under Section 11.9 lets each Ancillary Agreement control as to its subject matter. Nothing in the SPA shows that the IP Assignment Agreement defines 'Business' more narrowly as organic fluid milk only, or that it limits Assigned IP to that narrower Business. Without that, an associate could only note a general drafting dependency. They could not see that the yogurt recipes, starter cultures and the 'Brouloul Farmstead' cheese brand are left out and stay with Seller's affiliate. The narrower definition, which is the core of the problem, appears only in the IP Assignment Agreement.

ip_assignment_agreement_brouloul_farmste.evidence: "Business" means the production, processing and sale of organic fluid milk, as conducted by Assignee as of the date of the Purchase Agreement.
ip_assignment_agreement_brouloul_farmste.reason: On its own, this document shows that 'Business' is defined narrowly as fluid milk and that 'Assigned IP' covers only IP used in that Business. There is an internal oddity: Starter Cultures, including bacterial, yeast and mold cultures, are listed even though they have little use in fluid milk. That might make a careful associate suspect the target makes cultured products. But the document never says Kettlebrook makes yogurt, butter or cheese, and it never mentions a 'Brouloul Farmstead' cheese brand or yogurt recipes. It also does not show that the SPA defines 'Business' more broadly, that SPA Section 4.12 warrants only the Assigned IP, or that SPA Section 11.9 makes this agreement control. Without the SPA, the associate cannot tell whether the narrow definition leaves out any IP the client is paying for. So the gap, and the harm to the client, depend on the other document.

results.evidence: SPA Section 9.1(b): "The obligations of Seller under Section 9.2(b) shall survive until the Maturity Date (as defined in the Seller Note)." Seller Note Section 1.3: the Maturity Date is "the date that is eighteen (18) months after the Issue Date (the Closing Date)."
results.reason:
Read together, the two provisions cut off Seller's Pre-Closing Taxes indemnity 18 months after Closing. Seller gives that indemnity and Buyer, the firm's client, benefits from it. Tax authorities can usually assess the Company's 2024–2026 tax years for at least three years after filing, so Buyer would lose indemnity protection for assessments made after month 18.

The SPA offers no fallback:
- The tax rep in Section 4.14 is not a Fundamental Representation, so it survives only 15 months under Section 9.1(a).
- Section 9.1(c) preserves only claims asserted before the survival period expires.

The LOI (Section 5.2) recorded the agreed survival as 60 days after the applicable statute of limitations, so the 18-month cutoff departs from the deal terms. The emails show the SPA was signed on November 6, 2026, but Closing (targeted for December 1) has not occurred. The Seller Note is still being finalized and nothing shows the client accepted this outcome. Buyer can still raise it, for example by amending the SPA before Closing or by setting the Maturity Date and survival separately. The issue is present and actionable.

stock_purchase_agreement_kettlebrook.md.evidence: The obligations of Seller under Section 9.2(b) shall survive until the Maturity Date (as defined in the Seller Note).
stock_purchase_agreement_kettlebrook.md.reason: The SPA shows that the Pre-Closing Taxes indemnity in Section 9.2(b) ends on a date defined only in the Seller Note. It also shows that the Section 4.14 tax representation is not a Fundamental Representation and survives only 15 months. Read alone, though, linking survival to the note's maturity looks like a sensible match to Buyer's set-off security under Section 9.6. The SPA does not say when the Maturity Date falls. The fact that it is only 18 months after Closing, well short of the tax assessment limitations period, appears only in the Seller Note (D5). The LOI's agreed term of 60 days after the statute of limitations appears only in D4. An associate reading the SPA alone could note that the date depends on another document, but could not see that the period is too short or that it harms Buyer.

seller_note_lepund.md.evidence: The entire unpaid Principal Amount ... shall be due and payable in full on the date that is eighteen (18) months after the Issue Date (the Closing Date) (the "Maturity Date").
seller_note_lepund.md.reason: The Note sets the Maturity Date at 18 months after Closing. That is ordinary payment drafting. Section 5 also gives Buyer a set-off right for Article IX indemnity claims, but nothing in the Note says the tax indemnity's survival period is tied to the Maturity Date. That link appears only in SPA Section 9.1(b). Without it, an associate reading the Note alone would see a normal 18-month maturity and no cut-off of Buyer's pre-closing tax indemnity. The harm to the client, losing tax claims after 18 months when assessments can still come later, can't be seen from this document alone.

results.evidence: Section 8.2: "Recipient shall indemnify, defend and hold harmless Provider and its Affiliates ... from and against all Losses arising out of or relating to the provision of the Services or Recipient's use of the Services, except to the extent caused by Provider's willful misconduct." Section 8.4: "The aggregate liability of each party arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall not exceed the total Fees paid by Recipient under this Agreement. The limitations in Section 8.3 and this Section 8.4 shall not apply to Recipient's obligations under Section 8.2 or to Recipient's obligation to pay the Fees."
results.reason: The problem is present and actionable. Under 8.2 Lepund (Recipient, the client) indemnifies Seller for all Losses from the provision of the Services, carved back only for Provider's willful misconduct. That covers Seller's own ordinary and gross negligence in hauling, organic certification work and payroll. Section 8.4 removes both the fee cap and the 8.3 consequential-damages exclusion for that indemnity, so Lepund's exposure has no limit. Seller's indemnity under 8.1 reaches only gross negligence, willful misconduct and confidentiality breaches. Seller's overall liability is also capped at fees paid, which may be low early in the term. Section 8.4 also makes Seller's capped liability for its own Section 7 breaches lopsided against Lepund. SPA 11.9 makes the TSA control as to its subject matter, and nothing elsewhere in the folder cures this. The TSA is still a draft: signature packets are being circulated and closing is set for December 1, 2026. Lepund can therefore still negotiate the provision.

results.evidence: Section 12.3: "Recipient may not assign this Agreement or any of its rights or obligations hereunder without the prior written consent of Provider ... Provider may assign this Agreement, in whole or in part, or delegate the performance of any Service to any Person upon written notice to Recipient and without the consent of Recipient."
results.reason:
The assignment clause is one-sided against the client. Lepund, as Recipient, needs Provider's consent to assign. Brouloul, as Provider, may assign the TSA or delegate any Service to "any Person" on mere notice. Nothing excludes competitors, requires Recipient's consent, or keeps Provider liable after a full assignment.

The risk is concrete because of what an assignee would see. Under Section 5.1, Lepund must cause the Company to give Provider and Service Personnel access to producer pay prices, milk supply contracts, herd records and customer orders. A competing organic dairy processor that takes over the hauling or payroll Services would obtain that commercially sensitive data during the 9-month term.

The other documents do not cure this:
- SPA 6.4 (confidentiality) and SPA 6.5 (non-compete) bind only Seller and its Affiliates, not an unaffiliated assignee.
- SPA 11.4 restricts assignment of the SPA only, and SPA 11.9 makes the TSA control as to its subject matter.
- TSA Section 7 binds "Provider," but after a full assignment the competitor would itself become Provider.
- Section 4.2 (Provider remains responsible for Service Personnel) helps only for delegation, not outright assignment.

The TSA is unsigned and pre-closing (Closing is targeted for December 1, 2026), so the client can still negotiate this point. The problem is present and actionable.
